name: PCM1860DBT
title: 4-channel or 2-channel, 192-kHz audio ADCs with PGA (PCM1860 to PCM1865)
summary: The PCM186x family are stereo or four-channel audio ADCs running from a single 3.3 V supply, with sample rates from 8 kHz to 192 kHz. Each has a front-end MUX and PGA that take microphone-level signals up to 2.1 VRMS single-ended or 4.2 VRMS differential, an audio PLL, and a secondary ADC that detects signal presence and DC control levels for automatic system wake and sleep. The PCM1860 and PCM1861 are configured by pins; the PCM1862 to PCM1865 are programmed over I2C or SPI and add mixing, digital microphones and TDM output.
key_figures: 3.0 V to 3.6 V AVDD and DVDD; IOVDD 1.8 V or 3.3 V
80 mW 2-channel, 135.3 mW 4-channel active, typ at 3.3 V

circuits.title: Stereo microphone recording, hardware-controlled device in master mode
circuits.description: A PCM1860 or PCM1861 records two electret microphones. Mic Bias feeds each microphone through its own 2.2 kΩ resistor, and 10 µF capacitors carry the two microphone signals to input pair 1 (VINL1 and VINR1), single-ended. A crystal on XI and XO with 15 pF to ground clocks the part as audio master; BCK, LRCK and DOUT go to the system processor, which also watches INT and connects to SCKI. The MD pins are set by the system for rate and master/slave, filter, format, and input and gain. IOVDD and DVDD share one 3.3 V rail, AVDD has its own, and each rail has 0.1 µF and 10 µF to ground; LDO and VREF each have 2.2 µF.

parts.note: bias feed to the left microphone
bias feed to the right microphone
load capacitors chosen from the crystal's data

notes: X7R ceramic capacitors rated 6.3 V suit the supply rails.
The processor pin driving INT works as an interrupt input, or as an output driven high to power the device down.

circuits.title: Stereo microphone recording, software-controlled device in slave PLL mode with 1.8-V IOVDD
circuits.description: A PCM1862 to PCM1865 records two electret microphones biased from Mic Bias through 2.2 kΩ and coupled by 10 µF into input pair 1. The part is a clock slave to a 1.8-V host, for example a Bluetooth module, that gives BCK and LRCK and no master clock; the PLL makes the master clock from BCK, so XI, XO and SCKI are left open. MD0 is grounded to select I2C, MS/AD sets the address, and the four GPIO pins serve as interrupts or GPIO. IOVDD and LDO both sit on the 1.8 V rail, bypassing the internal LDO; DVDD and AVDD each take their own 3.3 V. Each rail has 0.1 µF and 10 µF, and LDO and VREF have 2.2 µF.

parts.note: bias feed to the left microphone
bias feed to the right microphone

notes: The host supplies BCK at 64 × fS so that the automatic PLL setting works.
Slave mode is set with MST_MODE (Page 0, 0x20).
X7R ceramic capacitors rated 6.3 V suit the supply rails.

circuits.title: Single 3.3-V supply
circuits.description: AVDD, DVDD and IOVDD share one 3.3 V rail with 10 µF to ground. LDO is an output and VREF a reference node, each decoupled to ground with 2.2 µF; DGND and AGND go to the same ground.
notes: AGND and DGND share one ground plane.

circuits.title: Single-ended line input
circuits.description: A 10 µF capacitor AC-couples a single-ended source to an analog input, which biases itself to AVDD / 2.
notes: Any VINLx or VINRx input pin takes this circuit; VINL1/VIN1P stands for it.

circuits.title: Single-ended line input with anti-aliasing filter
circuits.description: The source reaches the input pin through a 10 µF DC-blocking capacitor and a 100 Ω, 0.01 µF low-pass for anti-aliasing where there is much out-of-band noise. The resistor also limits current into the input ESD diodes when the input exceeds its range.

parts.note: film, close to the input pin, returned near AGND

notes: Any VINLx or VINRx input pin takes this circuit; VINL1/VIN1P stands for it.

circuits.title: Differential line input
circuits.description: Each leg of a differential source is AC-coupled by 10 µF into a P and M input pair.
notes: Any VINxP and VINxM pair takes this circuit; differential input 1 (VIN1P, VIN1M) stands for it.

circuits.title: Differential line input with anti-aliasing filter
circuits.description: Each leg of a differential source passes a 10 µF DC block and a 47 Ω resistor; a 0.01 µF capacitor across the two input pins completes the anti-aliasing low-pass. The two resistors are matched closely to hold common-mode rejection.

parts.note: film, across the inputs close to the pins

notes: Any VINxP and VINxM pair takes this circuit; differential input 1 (VIN1P, VIN1M) stands for it.

circuits.title: 3.3 V for all supplies
circuits.description: One 3.3 V rail feeds AVDD, DVDD and IOVDD; the internal LDO makes 1.8 V at the LDO pin, which carries a decoupling capacitor to ground. The rails carry their own decoupling capacitors in addition.

circuits.title: Separate 3.3 V for AVDD and DVDD
circuits.description: AVDD takes its own analog 3.3 V; DVDD and IOVDD share a digital 3.3 V. The LDO pin is the internal 1.8 V output with a decoupling capacitor. The device does not power up until both AVDD and DVDD are present, so the two rails may be separate.

circuits.title: 1.8-V IOVDD with 3.3 V for AVDD and DVDD
circuits.description: For 1.8-V processors and lower power, an external 1.8 V drives both IOVDD and LDO, which bypasses the internal LDO; the digital core then runs from IOVDD. AVDD and DVDD stay on 3.3 V, since parts of the digital core need 3.3 V.

equations.name: PLL output clock
equations.expr: PLLCK = PLLCKIN × R × J.D / P = PLLCKIN × R × K / P

where.PLLCKIN: PLL reference clock, 1 MHz to 50 MHz
where.D: fractional part of K to four digits, 0000 to 9999

equations.note: Limits are in the two equations that follow. Examples: K = 8.5 gives J = 8, D = 5000; K = 7.12 gives J = 7, D = 1200; K = 14.03 gives J = 14, D = 0300; K = 6.0004 gives J = 6, D = 0004.

equations.name: PLL limits, integer K (D = 0000)
equations.expr: 1 MHz ≤ PLLCKIN / P ≤ 20 MHz; 64 MHz < PLLCKIN × K × R / P < 100 MHz; 1 ≤ J ≤ 63

equations.name: PLL limits, fractional K (D ≠ 0000)
equations.expr: 6.667 MHz ≤ PLLCKIN / P ≤ 20 MHz; 64 MHz < PLLCKIN × K × R / P < 100 MHz; 4 ≤ J ≤ 11; R = 1

equations.name: Reference sample rate from the PLL

where.N: divider chosen so that fSref × N = PLLCKIN × K × R / P falls in the allowed range

equations.name: Fade time
equations.note: Without a zero crossing for 8192 / fS, the fade is forced over 48 / fS.

operation.text: Six parts share one TSSOP-30 footprint. The PCM1860 and PCM1861 are set by pins (MD0 to MD6) and give two channels; the PCM1862 and PCM1863 (two channels) and PCM1864 and PCM1865 (four channels) are set over I2C or SPI. The odd numbers have the 110 dB SNR grade, the even numbers 103 dB.

Inputs accept 2.1 VRMS single-ended or 4.2 VRMS differential (2.1 VRMS on each pin, in antiphase). A MUX (and, on software parts, a mixer) ahead of the PGA picks or sums inputs; there is no separate gain before the PGA. The input pins bias themselves to AVDD / 2, so each needs a DC-blocking capacitor, also when an amplifier drives it. Leave unused analog inputs unconnected.
The input clamp diodes are to carry as little current as possible, with about 5 mA as the absolute limit; a series resistor ahead of the pin limits it.

Analog microphones are handled like line inputs plus bias. Mic Bias (pin 5) gives 2.6 V for electret microphones and is decoupled or filtered with an external capacitor; it may be left open when unused. Its regulator and an on-chip resistor to ground are set by MIC_BIAS_CTRL (Page 3, 0x15); the resistor is bypassed by default. Hardware parts offer 0, 12 or 32 dB; software parts -12 dB to +32 dB.

PDM microphones are supported on the software parts only: two on the PCM1862 and PCM1863 (data on GPIO1), four on the PCM1864 and PCM1865 (data on GPIO0 and GPIO1, clock from GPIO2). Two microphones share a data line, one driving it on each clock edge. The microphone clock is 2.048 MHz at 32 kHz, 2.8224 MHz at 44.1 kHz, 3.072 MHz at 48 kHz (64 × fS) or 96 kHz (32 × fS). Recommended: fS of 32 or 44.1 kHz, SCK of 256 × fS, automatic clock detection on. Digital gain in this mode reaches 18 dB (mixer) on the 2-channel parts and 30 dB (mixer plus 12 dB digital PGA) on the 4-channel parts. The microphones are powered externally.

Gain is split between an analog PGA (1 dB steps from -12 to +12 dB, then 20 and 32 dB) and a digital PGA for half-dB steps and for 12 to 20 dB. One register per channel sets the total and the device divides it (18 dB becomes 12 dB analog plus 6 dB digital); this auto mapping can be turned off (PGA_MODE, Page 0, 0x19), which is how digital microphone gain is set; manual digital gain works on the 4-channel parts only. Gain steps toward the target in 0.5 dB steps at zero crossings, which needs the DSP clocked, so in slave mode the host clocks must be running. Mixer gain changes take effect at once.
Each 0.5 dB step is made when the oversampled input crosses zero (sampled at four times fS); after 8192 samples without one, the gain steps once per sample.

On software parts the gain can drop automatically in 0.5 dB steps after a set number of clipped samples is seen after the decimation filter, down to -3, -4, -5 or -6 dB, and an interrupt tells the host, which decides whether to raise the gain again. Linking the channels keeps a stereo pair balanced.

Software parts can take I2S data on GPIO0 to GPIO3 (GPIO_FUNC, Page 0, 0x10 and 0x11) and mix it with the ADC data in DSP2. The incoming data must be synchronous to the device clocks; there is no sample-rate converter. Clock contention with a source that drives the clock pins causes no damage but gives bad output; set the device as slave first.

The device needs a master clock, BCK and LRCK. It can be clock master (BCK and LRCK divided from a crystal or a CMOS clock) or slave. The master clock can come from a 15 to 35 MHz crystal on XI/XO, a 3.3-V CMOS clock on SCKI, or a 1.8-V CMOS clock on XI; XI and SCKI are combined internally. A PLL makes audio clocks from any 1 to 50 MHz source. Hardware parts in slave mode make their own master clock from BCK when none is given.

MD0 and MD1 select slave mode (256, 384 or 512 × fS detected) or master at 512, 384 or 256 × fS. In master mode BCK is 64 per LRCK, up to 32 bits a channel; in slave mode BCK is also to be 64 × fS. With a crystal the top rate is 96 kHz (24.576 MHz / 256); 192 kHz needs an external CMOS clock. A hardware part in crystal master mode cannot switch to external slave mode.

Automatic clock configuration (CLKDET_EN, Page 0, 0x20) is on by default and sets the dividers from the detected rates. In BCK-input slave PLL mode the PLL makes the master clock from BCK. In non-audio MCK mode (for example a shared 12, 24 or 27 MHz clock) automatic configuration is turned off and the PLL is set by hand in Page 0, 0x28 to 0x2D, and the clock tree is set to take its master-mode SCKOUT from the PLL, with the dividers from SCK down to BCK and from BCK down to LRCK chosen to suit. The crystal oscillator can feed the PLL on software parts only. 8 kHz needs an external MCK; the autodetect and PLL work down to 32 kHz.

PLL enable is Page 0, 0x28 bit 0; P is 0x29 bits 3:0; R is 0x2A bits 3:0; J is 0x2B bits 5:0; D is 14 bits, MSBs in 0x2D bits 5:0 and LSBs in 0x2C bits 7:0, and takes effect when the LSB byte is written. The PLL is on by default because the DSPs need a high clock.

A clock monitor checks BCK per LRCK and the rates against an internal oscillator. On a clock error the device mutes at once, waits for good clocks, re-runs detection and reconfigures the PLL and dividers, then fades in. If every clock stops it goes to sleep and starts energysense detection. Status is in CLK_ERR_STAT and STATE (Page 0, 0x72 to 0x75). With a non-audio SCK the SCK error check is avoided by turning off CLKDET_EN.

In slave mode with automatic configuration, hold the clocks (or leave them high impedance) for at least 3 BCK periods, change them, then allow about 100 µs for reconfiguration; data then ramps back in at a zero crossing. In master mode, changing the MD pins or the rate register changes the rate.

Every main ADC is paired with one PGA and one MUX. ADC1L (and ADC2L on the 4-channel parts) sees the VINLx pins, ADC1R (and ADC2R) the VINRx pins. Left inputs can be mixed with each other in the left MUX and right with right; left-plus-right mono mixes are made in the digital mixer. The MSB of each input-select register inverts polarity.

A low-power one-bit delta-sigma ADC watches the inputs for energysense (signal level) and controlsense (DC level, for example a battery or a potentiometer). It runs from the audio clocks when active and from an on-chip oscillator in sleep. In sleep every input is single-ended and all eight are scanned in turn, each set for energysense or controlsense; in active mode energysense works only on the primary channel and other inputs are read through controlsense. An input attenuation limits controlsense to about 4.3 V. Its input impedance is 20 kΩ. Its response is not flat with frequency; LPF and HPF biquads in DSP memory can flatten it.

Each of the eight inputs has a reference level and a difference level; crossing the difference raises an interrupt, in active and sleep modes. No high-pass filter is applied. In sleep the device scans the controlsense inputs itself; in active mode the host steps SEC_ADC_INPUT_SEL (Page 0, 0x0A). Readings are 8-bit (SIGDET_DC_LEVEL registers, with DC_NOLATCH set in 0x58 and the inputs set as controlsense in 0x30), 16-bit two's complement through the latch in 0x58 to 0x5A, or streamed in TDM.

Energysense helps a host meet standby limits by flagging when audio stops and starts; the device never changes state on its own. Signal loss (software parts only): in active mode, an interrupt fires when the input stays below a threshold (for example -60 dB) for a set time (SIGDET_LOSS_TIME, Page 0, 0x33, 1 minute by default at 48 kHz; halved at 96 kHz, quartered at 192 kHz) and repeats per SIGDET_INT_INTVL (0x36) until reset. Signal resume: in sleep, an interrupt fires when an input rises above the threshold, -57 dBFS by default. Both thresholds are DSP coefficients set through Page 1. The interrupt can be pulsed or sticky (INT_PLS, 0x62).

In sleep each channel is watched for 160 ms (down to 50 Hz), 80 ms (100 Hz) or 40 ms (200 Hz); longer scans catch lower frequencies. All eight channels are scanned even when their interrupts are masked.

Two fixed-function DSPs do decimation, mixing, level detection and housekeeping; their coefficients are written indirectly through Page 1. The decimation filter is a classic FIR or a low-latency IIR; a DC-removing high-pass filter is on by default (DSP_CTRL, Page 0, 0x71). On hardware parts MD3 picks the filter, and a change needs a power cycle.

Four mixers combine ADC channels and incoming I2S data with gains from -120 dB to +18 dB in 4.20 format; a negative (two's complement) coefficient inverts phase. Coefficients act at once, with no soft ramp. Using the I2S input costs two digital microphone channels.

Select register page 1 through register 0x00, write the coefficient address to 0x02, the data to 0x04 to 0x06, then set the write request in 0x01; for example the resume threshold at -30 dB is 0x040C37 at address 0x2D.

DOUT fades in and out with an S-shaped curve at zero crossings on power up and down and on mute and unmute, 48 steps from mute to 0 dB. The fade takes 48 / fIN; without a zero crossing for 8192 / fS it is forced over 48 / fS.

On software parts each GPIO can be an input, an input with toggle detection, a sticky flag or an open-drain output (so interrupt lines can be wired together), with selectable polarity. Interrupts can come from energysense (loss or detection), controlsense, clipping after the PGA, or a toggling DIN. On the PCM1860 and PCM1861 the only interrupt is energysense detect on INT.

Hardware parts give 24-bit I2S (MD4 low) or left-justified (MD4 high). Software parts add right-justified and TDM (I2S_FMT, Page 0, 0x0B), with transmit and receive offsets in 0x0D and 0x0E. The 4-channel software parts can output a second DOUT on a GPIO, synchronous with the first; not in TDM.

TDM works in master and slave modes with 256 BCK per frame, carrying two to four mixer channels per device, plus the secondary ADC on channels five and six. LRCK is a 50 % frame or a one-bit pulse (master gives 50 % only; a slave needs only a rising edge). Words are 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits (24 data bits plus 8 zero bits); shorter words are truncated, not dithered. DOUT is high impedance outside its own slots. BCK period is to be at least 1 / (512 × fS). Two devices make eight channels: one master with the clock source, one slave on channels 5 to 8 clocked by its PLL.
Active: full operation. Idle: output muted, analog kept powered. Sleep: main ADCs off, energysense running. Standby: only the control port alive.

The host drives INT high (when no interrupt is pending) to idle the device and releases it (input or high impedance) to resume; while the device drives an interrupt, outside drive on INT is ignored. Stopping BCK and LRCK enters sleep; restarting them returns to active.
PWRDN_CTRL (Page 0, 0x70) enters and leaves standby and sleep; in slave mode stopping and restarting BCK and LRCK also enters and leaves sleep.
Driving IOVDD and LDO together with 1.8 V bypasses the LDO to save power. IOVDD must then be 1.8 V. BCK and data are then limited to 25 MHz, so TDM is limited to 96 kHz.

Software parts use I2C when MD0 is low or open and SPI when it is high. In I2C mode pin 25 (AD) picks address 0x94 or 0x96 (7-bit address 100101x); two devices can share a bus. The I2C port is a slave at 100 kHz or 400 kHz and works with no audio clocks present.

SPI is 4-wire (MS, MC, MOSI, MISO), independent of the audio clocks. Each access is 16 bits with MS low: 7 address bits, R/W (1 = read), then 8 data bits; data shifts on MC. On a read, MISO carries the data from clock 9 on; a write latches after the sixteenth. MS returns high between accesses. MISO can be reassigned as GPIO1 when reads are not needed.
Page 0 registers 0x72 to 0x75 and 0x78 report the device state, sample rate, clock ratios, clock errors and supply status at any time.

AVDD feeds the analog circuits, DVDD the 3.3-V clock circuits (PLL, oscillator), and IOVDD the I/O and the internal 1.8-V LDO for the digital core. AVDD and DVDD can be tied with little effect on performance; the device waits for both. Every part handles 1.8-V I/O when IOVDD and LDO are both fed 1.8 V.
There is no brownout detector and no reset pin; the supplies must meet their minimums.

Power-on reset brings up AVDD, DVDD and IOVDD, checks whether LDO is driven externally, enables the LDO if needed and releases the digital reset; the device then waits for the reference, configures the clocks (the PLL needs under 250 µs) and fades in the ADC output.

Standby at 3.3 V can reach 0.59 mW: write 0x70 = 0x14 on page 0, then 0x12 = 0x41 on page 3. Sleep can reach 14 mW at 3.3 V or 11.15 mW with 1.8-V IOVDD: with clocks running write 0x70 = 0x72 on page 0 and 0x14 = 0x10 on page 253, then stop the clocks (at 1.8-V levels when IOVDD is 1.8 V).

Keep analog and digital apart and route analog traces away from digital ones; pins 1 to 8 face the analog side and the rest the digital side. Use one shared ground plane for AGND and DGND; split planes are not needed. Put decoupling capacitors close to the supply pins on the device's side of the board with no vias between, and put ground between input traces for least crosstalk. Keep digital return currents away from AGND and the inputs. A two-layer board is enough.
Anti-aliasing capacitors (0.01 µF film) go as close as possible to the input pins, and their ground returns as close as possible to AGND.
A crystal goes on XI and XO with capacitors to ground as its maker suggests, typically 15 pF. A clock source not tied to an audio rate (for example a 12 MHz USB crystal) needs the PLL set by hand.
